- Resources flow **net from poorer to richer** countries
- Per unit of resource exported, rich countries earn **far more**
- The costs of extraction stay **where the extraction happens**

::: {.grid2 .stats .fragment}
::: {.cap}
[11×]{.statnum}

value added per **tonne of raw material** embodied in exports — in **high-income** compared with **lowest-income** countries
:::

::: {.cap}
[28×]{.statnum}

value added per **hour of labour** embodied in exports — in **high-income** compared with **lowest-income** countries
:::
:::

::: {.arrow .lg .fragment}
Where those costs are contested: **ecological distribution conflicts**
:::

environmentally extended multi-regional input-output model, 1990–2015;
net flows of materials, energy, land and labour to high-income countries.

## The environmentalism of the poor


::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="48%"}
::: {.colhead}
Ecological distribution conflicts
:::

- A growing **social metabolism** needs ever more materials, energy and sinks
- Conflicts over **who gets** the benefits and **who bears** the burdens
- Fought out in different **valuation languages**: money, livelihood, territory, sacredness
:::

::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.colhead}
Three currents of environmentalism
:::

- **Cult of wilderness**: protect pristine nature
- **Gospel of eco-efficiency**: green growth, technology, markets
- **Environmentalism of the poor**: livelihoods, territory and health of those living off the land
:::
:::

::: {.source}
Martínez-Alier [-@martinezalier2002]; Martínez-Alier et al. [-@martinezalier2010];
Anguelovski & Martínez-Alier [-@anguelovski2014]. Recall Text 3 of Session 2 [@martinezalier2015].
:::

## The EJAtlas: a global inventory of conflicts

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
- **Co-produced** by researchers and activist groups
- Every case **coded on one template**:
  - commodity and type of project
  - actors and mobilising groups
  - forms of mobilisation, intensity
  - impacts and outcome
- For you: **a starting point** for your country
:::

## What the cases show globally

::: {.grid3}
::: {.cap .fragment}
[Who mobilises]{.caphead}

Mostly vulnerable groups, mostly non-violent protest — in countries of **all income levels**
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[At what risk]{.caphead}

Criminalisation **20%**, physical violence **18%**, assassinations **13%** of cases
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[With what effect]{.caphead}

Projects stopped in **11%** of cases — up to **27%** with preventive mobilisation, diverse protest and litigation
:::
:::

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Indigenous Peoples: about **6%** of the world population — involved in at least **34%** of documented conflicts
:::

::: {.source}
Percentages of all cases analysed: 2,743 EJAtlas conflicts in Scheidel et al. [-@scheidel2020];
3,081 EJAtlas conflicts over development projects in Scheidel et al. [-@scheidel2023].
6% = share of Indigenous Peoples in the world population (6.2%).
:::

## Analysing a conflict: seven questions

     when; the sub-questions follow the EJAtlas coding template. -->

<tbody>

<tr class="fragment"><td>3</td><td><strong>Through whom?</strong> Actors</td><td>Companies, state, financiers, mobilising groups — who holds power?</td><td>Scheidel et al. (2018); Temper et al. (2015)</td></tr>

## Worked example: lithium in the Salar de Atacama, Chile


::: {.columns style="gap: 1.6em;"}
::: {.column width="44%"}
- **What, where:** lithium from brine, pumped from beneath the salt flat; operations since 1984 and 1996
- **Why:** brine pumped into evaporation ponds, plus freshwater — authorised quotas of about **2,000 l/s** of brine and **260 l/s** of freshwater
- **Through whom:** SQM and Albemarle, under contracts with the state agency CORFO — on the territories of the **Atacameño/Lickanantay**
:::

::: {.column width="56%"}
![](figures/fig_L06a_lithium_trade.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Chile supplies 73% of world lithium carbonate exports; 72% of Chile's exports go to China, followed by South Korea and Japan"}
:::
:::

::: {.source}
Flores Fernández & Alba [-@floresfernandez2023], quotas: SQM 1,600 + 240 l/s, Albemarle 442 + 23.5 l/s
(approved, not necessarily extracted). Trade: Atlas of Economic Complexity, 2024.
:::

## Worked example: lithium in the Salar de Atacama, Chile


- **Impacts:** high-Andean wetlands, vegetation and flamingo populations under pressure
  - **High scientific uncertainty** about the water balance — even after 30 years of extraction
- **Valuation languages:** state and companies treat brine as a **mineral**; Lickanantay communities insist it is **water** — and water is sacred
- **Mobilisation and outcome:** objections of Peine, Toconao, Socaire excluded on formal grounds (2006)
  - Communities' council intervenes against SQM and the 2018 CORFO contract
  - Excess extraction found — **no sanction**, a compliance plan instead
- **Not one voice:** resistance *and* negotiation
  - Substantial direct and indirect economic benefits from the companies
  - Some members work in the mines
- **So what:** "green extractivism" — the **colonial shadow of green electromobility**

::: {.source}
Flores Fernández & Alba [-@floresfernandez2023]; Jerez Henríquez, Garcés & Torres Salinas [-@jerez2021].
:::

## Read the atlas critically

- It records conflicts that were **documented** — often by those mobilising
- Coverage is **uneven** across countries — gaps e.g. in Central Asia, Russia, the Pacific
- **No entry is not no conflict**
- So: triangulate with **peer-reviewed case studies** and local sources

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Same lesson as Session 3: the vantage point decides what is in the picture
:::

::: {.source}
Temper, Del Bene & Martínez-Alier [-@temper2015]; on data gaps, Scheidel et al. [-@scheidel2023].
:::

## Summary

- Ecologically unequal exchange becomes visible as **ecological distribution conflicts** where resources are extracted
- **Environmentalism of the poor**: defending livelihoods, territory and health — not a luxury
- The **EJAtlas**: a global, co-produced inventory — a starting point, to be read critically
- **Seven questions** for a single conflict: what and where, why, through whom, impacts, how, when — and so what
- The Atacama case: even **"green" technologies** have extraction frontiers and contested valuation languages
- Next: **measuring** the embodied flows → after the break; **justice** → Session 9

## Suggestion for country analysis

<!-- From L05 (slide 29 of the PDF), plus the EJAtlas bullet. -->

- Look at data on trade, and trade openness
- Complement this with data on export composition, complexity, and the product space
- What is your country specialized in?
- What are the outlooks for the future?
- Which **environmental conflicts** does the EJAtlas list for your country? Analyse one with the **seven questions**
